paragraphs: Nature sets limits to the stature of a well-formed man and, beyond those limits, produces only giants or dwarfs. In the same way, for a State to have the best possible constitution, one can fix limits that keep it from being too large to be well governed and too small to maintain itself. Every body politic has a _maximum_ strength that it cannot exceed and that it only loses by growing larger. The more the social tie is stretched, the looser it becomes; and in general a small State is stronger, in proportion to its size, than a large one.

A thousand arguments can be offered for this principle. First, long distances make administration harder, just as a weight grows heavier at the end of a longer lever. Administration therefore becomes more burdensome as the distance increases. For, to begin with, each city has its own administration, paid for by the people; each district has its own, again paid for by the people; then comes each province, and then the great governments, satrapies and viceroyalties, which cost more the higher one goes, and always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last of all comes the supreme administration, which swallows up all the rest. All this extra expense is a continual drain on the subjects. Far from being better governed by all these different levels, they are worse governed than if there were a single authority over them. Meanwhile there are scarcely resources left to meet emergencies, and when these must be drawn on, the State is always on the brink of destruction.

This is not all. Not only does the government have less vigor and speed in securing obedience to the laws, preventing nuisances, correcting abuses and guarding against rebellious schemes begun in distant places; the people also feel less affection for their rulers, whom they never see, for their country, which seems to them like the whole world, and for their fellow citizens, most of whom they do not know. The same laws cannot suit so many different provinces, with different customs, in the most varied climates, unable to bear a uniform government. Different laws only cause trouble and confusion among peoples who live under the same rulers, are in constant contact, mix and intermarry, and, coming under the sway of new customs, never know whether they can call even their own inheritance their own. Talent is buried, virtue unknown and vice unpunished, among such a multitude of men who do not know one another, gathered together in one place at the seat of the central administration. The leaders, overwhelmed with business, see nothing for themselves; the State is governed by clerks. Finally, the measures needed to maintain the general authority, which all these distant officials want either to evade or to take advantage of, absorb all the energy of the public, so that none is left for the happiness of the people. There is hardly enough to defend it when need arises, and so a body too big for its constitution gives way and falls, crushed under its own weight.

Again, the State must give itself a secure foundation if it is to be stable, to withstand the shocks it cannot help suffering, and to bear the efforts it will be forced to make to sustain itself. For all peoples have a kind of centrifugal force that makes them constantly act against one another and tend to grow at their neighbors’ expense, like the vortices of Descartes. The weak therefore risk being swallowed up soon, and it is almost impossible for any State to preserve itself except by putting itself in a kind of equilibrium with all the others, so that the pressure on it is practically equal on every side.

We can therefore see that there are reasons for expansion and reasons for contraction, and it is no small part of the statesman’s skill to find, between them, the mean most favorable to the preservation of the State. It can be said that the reason for expansion, being merely external and relative, ought to be subordinate to the reasons for contraction, which are internal and absolute. A strong and healthy constitution is the first thing to look for, and it is better to count on the vigor that comes from good government than on the resources a large territory supplies.

It may be added that some States are known to have been so constituted that the necessity of making conquests was part of their very constitution, and that to maintain themselves they were forced to expand ceaselessly. Perhaps they congratulated themselves greatly on this fortunate necessity, which nonetheless showed them, along with the limit of their greatness, the inevitable moment of their fall.
